usage: casual possessive 내; the polite form is 제 방
subject 이; 좁다 is the natural opposite of 넓다 for rooms
static location takes 에 with 있다
action done inside a place takes 에서
examples: 여기가 제 방이에요.
This is my room.
서술격 조사 이에요 after a consonant; introducing a space
방에서 친구하고 게임해요.
I play games with a friend in my room.
action location 에서, not 에, because something is happening there
방이 너무 좁아서 침대만 있어요.
The room is so small that there's only a bed.
-아서 gives the reason; 좁다 (cramped) vs 작다 (small in size)
nuance: 방 is the Sino-Korean character 房 ('room, chamber') and is the all-purpose word for any enclosed room, and it builds dozens of everyday compounds: 안방 (master/main room), 공부방 (study room), 노래방 (singing room/karaoke), 찜질방 (Korean sauna room), and PC방 (internet cafe). The key contrast to fix in your head is 방 vs 집: 집 is the whole house/home, but 방 is just one room inside it, so 'I'm going home' must be 집에 가요, never 방에 가요. The grammar trap is the 에 vs 에서 split: merely being located in the room uses 에 (방에 있어요 = it's in the room), but any action carried out inside the room uses 에서 (방에서 공부해요 = I study in my room) — English 'in the room' blurs both, and overusing 에 for actions is the #1 beginner error. Collocations: 방을 치우다/정리하다 (tidy the room), 방이 좁다 (the room is cramped). Register is fully neutral, used by everyone.

mistakes: Saying 방에서 있어요 for 'it's in the room.' Existence/location with 있다 takes 에 (방에 있어요); 에서 is only for actions performed there.
Translating 'I'm going home' as 방에 가요. 방 is a single room, not the home as a whole — use 집에 가요.
Pairing 작다 with rooms to mean 'cramped.' For a tight room Koreans prefer 방이 좁아요 (narrow/cramped); 작다 sounds like the room's dimensions are literally tiny.

usage: transitive: the door is the object 을, you act on it
pair verb to 열다; both take 을
intransitive 열리다: subject 이, no agent
collocation for knocking rather than 치다
examples: 문 좀 닫아 주세요.
Please close the door.
좀 softens the request; -아 주세요 = do it for me, politely
바람 때문에 문이 저절로 닫혔어요.
The door closed by itself because of the wind.
intransitive 닫히다 + 저절로 (on its own); no one closed it
택배 기사님이 문을 두드렸어요.
The delivery driver knocked on the door.
두드리다 is the set verb for knocking on a door
nuance: 문 is the Sino-Korean 門 ('gate, door') and covers both interior doors and outer gates, feeding compounds like 정문 (main gate), 후문 (back gate), 대문 (front gate of a house), and even 창문 (window, lit. 'window-door'). The crucial grammar point for English speakers is the transitive/intransitive pair: 열다/닫다 are things YOU do to the door (문을 열어요 = I open it, object 을), whereas 열리다/닫히다 describe the door doing it on its own or in a resulting state (문이 열려요 = the door opens, subject 이). English uses 'open' for both, so learners wrongly say 문이 열어요; pick the verb by whether there's an actor. Also distinguish 문 (the physical door) from 입구 (entrance/way in) — 입구 is the opening/access point, 문 is the panel itself. Register is neutral.

Confusing 문 and 입구. 입구 is the entrance/opening you walk through; 문 is the actual door. '정문 앞에서 만나요' (the main gate) ≠ '입구에서 만나요' (the entrance area).

usage: object 을; same 열다/닫다 verbs as 문
spatial noun 밖 + 에 for the view beyond
to come in through the window
examples: 창문 좀 열어도 돼요?
May I open the window?
-아도 돼요 asks permission; 좀 softens it
햇빛이 창문으로 들어와요.
Sunlight comes in through the window.
으로 = the route/path the light travels
창문 밖에 눈이 와요.
It's snowing outside the window.
밖에 (outside) describes the scene beyond the glass
nuance: 창문 is a compound of 창 (Sino-Korean 窓, 'window') + 문 (門, 'door'), literally 'window-door,' and it's the everyday spoken word; the bare 창 survives mainly in compounds and writing (유리창 'glass pane', 창가 'by the window', 차창 'car window') and sounds more literary alone. The big English-speaker trap is the particle: 'look through the window' uses 으로 to mark the route the gaze or light takes (창문으로 봐요), NOT 에 — English 'through' maps to directional 으로 here. Note 창문 takes the same transitive verbs as a door (열다/닫다), since it literally contains 문. Don't confuse 창문 with 거울 (mirror), which beginners sometimes mix up because both are flat glass surfaces on a wall. Register is fully neutral and used by all ages.

mistakes: Saying 창문에 하늘을 봐요 for 'I look at the sky through the window.' The window is the route, so use directional 창문으로 봐요; 에 would mark a static location.
Using bare 창 in casual speech, e.g. 창을 열어요. It sounds bookish — in conversation Koreans say 창문을 열어요.
Treating 창문 as opening intransitively: 창문이 열어요 is wrong. Use 창문이 열려요 (the window opens) for the passive, like 문.

usage: to lie down on the bed
to get up out of bed
starting point of the motion 에서
examples: 저는 침대에서 안 자고 바닥에서 자요.
I don't sleep in a bed, I sleep on the floor.
contrast 에서…에서; many Koreans sleep on 이불 on the floor
피곤해서 침대에 누웠어요.
I was tired so I lay down on the bed.
눕다 → 누웠어요 (ㅂ-irregular past); 에 marks where you end up resting
아침에 침대에서 일어나기 힘들어요.
It's hard to get out of bed in the morning.
에서 = the point you rise from; -기 힘들다 = hard to do
nuance: 침대 is Sino-Korean 寢臺 ('sleep-platform/stand') and specifically means a raised Western-style bed frame with a mattress; traditional Korean homes sleep on 이불 (bedding/duvet) laid on a warm 온돌 floor, so 침대 is not a universal given. The grammar trap is the 에 vs 에서 contrast tied to the verb: 눕다 (lie down) and 자다 vs the act — use 에 for reaching a resting position (침대에 누워요, you settle ONTO it) but 에서 for an activity carried out there (침대에서 자요, 침대에서 책을 읽어요). English 'on/in the bed' erases this. Contrast 침대 with 소파 (sofa) and 이불 (floor bedding): a foreigner saying '침대에서 자요' is fine, but describing Korean-style floor sleeping needs 바닥에서 자요 or 이불에서 자요. The set verb for making a bed is 침대를 정리하다, never 만들다 (which means to build one).

Using 침대를 만들어요 to mean 'I make the bed.' 만들다 = construct/build. To tidy the bedding say 침대를 정리해요.
Assuming everyone uses a 침대. To describe floor sleeping on bedding, use 이불 or 바닥에서 자요, not 침대.

usage: resting destination 에 with 앉다, never 에서
to stand up from the chair
starting point of the motion 에서
collocation 빼다 (pull out) for offering a seat
examples: 여기 의자에 앉으세요.
Please have a seat on this chair.
앉다 + -으세요 honorific; 에 marks where you come to rest
회의 끝나고 의자에서 일어났어요.
After the meeting I stood up from my chair.
에서 = the point you rise from; motion away
이 의자가 푹신하고 편해요.
This chair is plush and comfortable.
푹신하다 (soft/plush) + 편하다 collocate for seating
nuance: 의자 is Sino-Korean 椅子 ('chair') and covers any seat with legs — dining chairs, office chairs (사무용 의자 or 사무 의자), folding chairs (접이식 의자). The single most common English-speaker error is the particle with 앉다: sitting DOWN is reaching a resting position, so it must be 의자에 앉아요 (에 = destination), not 의자에서 앉아요 — even though English 'sit ON the chair' tempts you toward a location particle. Compare with standing up, which is motion away and DOES take 에서: 의자에서 일어나요. Distinguish 의자 (chair, you sit on it) from 소파 (sofa/couch, plush multi-seat) and 책상 (desk) — beginners sometimes pair them loosely. The set phrase for offering someone a seat is 의자를 빼 드리다 (pull the chair out for them). Register is neutral.

Calling a sofa 의자. A plush multi-seat couch is 소파; 의자 is a single hard-ish chair.
Using 위에 redundantly: 의자 위에 앉아요 sounds odd for normal sitting. Just say 의자에 앉아요 — 위에 is for objects placed on top of the seat.

usage: action at the desk takes 에서
위 (top) + 에 for objects placed on it
에 marks settling at the desk to work
examples: 책상 위에 노트북이 있어요.
There's a laptop on the desk.
위에 = on top of; 있다 for existence
조용한 카페보다 책상에서 더 잘 집중돼요.
I concentrate better at my desk than in a quiet cafe.
에서 = where the activity (focusing) happens; 보다 compares
시험 전에 책상을 깨끗이 정리했어요.
I tidied my desk neatly before the exam.
정리하다 + 깨끗이 (neatly); the set verb for clearing a desk
nuance: 책상 literally combines 책 (book, 冊) + 상 (low table/stand, 床), i.e. a 'book-table' — a desk for studying or working, which is exactly why you must NOT use it for a dining table: that is 식탁 ('eating-table', 食卓). English 'table' lumps these together and causes the classic mistake of saying 책상 at a restaurant. The location particle splits the usual way: an action performed at the desk takes 에서 (책상에서 공부해요, 책상에서 일해요), while an object resting on its surface takes 위 + 에 (책상 위에 컵이 있어요). Also separate 책상 (a working desk) from 탁자 (a small side/coffee table) and 식탁 (dining table). The set verb for clearing/organizing a desk is 정리하다, not 청소하다 (청소 is more about cleaning floors/dirt). Register is neutral.

Using 에 for the activity: 책상에 공부해요 is incorrect. Studying is an action, so use 책상에서 공부해요. Reserve 에 for sitting down (책상에 앉아요).
Saying 책상을 청소해요 for tidying papers on it. To clear/organize the desktop use 책상을 정리해요; 청소 implies scrubbing dirt.

usage: 입다 is the body-clothing verb; object 을
pair verb to 입다 for the torso/body
어울리다 collocation for looking good on you
examples: 오늘 뭐 입을까요?
What should I wear today?
입다 + -ㄹ까요 (shall I/what shall); 옷 is implied, not stated
땀이 나서 옷을 갈아입었어요.
I sweated so I changed my clothes.
갈아입다 → 갈아입었어요; -아서 gives the reason
그 옷이 너한테 정말 잘 어울려.
Those clothes really suit you.
반말; 어울리다 = suit/look good on; 한테 = on/to you
nuance: 옷 is a pure native Korean word (no hanja) meaning clothes/clothing for the body, and the verb you MUST pair it with is 입다 (to wear on the torso/body) — never 신다, which is reserved for footwear on the feet (신발을 신다), nor 쓰다 (hats/glasses) nor 끼다 (gloves/rings). English 'wear/put on' covers every garment with one verb, so this split is the central pitfall: 옷을 신어요 is a classic beginner error. To take clothes off is 벗다, to change them 갈아입다. For 'these clothes look good on you,' Korean says 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), not a direct translation of 'you look good.' Note 옷 is treated as singular/uncountable grammatically (no plural needed): one outfit or a wardrobe full is still just 옷. The dressier counterpart 의상 (costume/attire, 衣裳) is for performances or formal contexts. Register is neutral and everyday.

usage: 신다 is the footwear verb; object 을
벗다 for removing shoes/clothes; key at the entrance
갈아 신다 (change-wear) parallels 갈아입다 for clothes
맞다 (fit) collocation; 발에 = to the feet
examples: 들어올 때 신발 벗어 주세요.
Please take your shoes off when you come in.
-을 때 = when; removing shoes indoors is the norm in Korea
새 신발이 발에 안 맞아서 불편해요.
The new shoes don't fit my feet so they're uncomfortable.
맞다 (fit) + -아서; 불편하다 (uncomfortable) for shoes
운동하러 갈 때 운동화로 갈아 신어요.
When I go exercise I change into sneakers.
갈아 신다 = swap shoes; 운동화 (sneakers) is a type of 신발
nuance: 신발 is native Korean (built from the verb root 신- 'to wear on feet' + 발 'foot') and means footwear in general — 운동화 (sneakers), 구두 (dress shoes), 슬리퍼 (slippers) are all 신발. The verb it demands is 신다, used ONLY for things on the feet, which is the mirror-image trap to 옷: just as you can't say 옷을 신다, you can't say 신발을 입다. English 'put on' hides the distinction, so 신발을 입어요 is a frequent beginner slip. Removing shoes is 벗다 — and culturally this matters enormously, since you always take shoes off before entering a Korean home (집에 들어갈 때 신발을 벗어요). For fit, use 맞다 (신발이 발에 맞아요), not 맞추다 (which means to have something custom-made). Changing shoes is 갈아 신다, parallel to 갈아입다 for clothes. Register is neutral and everyday.

usage: to carry a bag on the shoulder/back
메다 for backpacks/shoulder bags slung on you
to carry a bag in the hand
들다 for hand-held bags; contrast with 메다
안 (inside) + 에 to specify the interior
examples: 책을 가방에 넣었어요.
I put the book into the bag.
넣다 → 넣었어요; 에 marks where it goes in
가방이 너무 무거워서 어깨가 아파요.
The bag is so heavy my shoulder hurts.
무겁다 (heavy, ㅂ-irregular) + -아서; common with 메다 bags
오늘은 백팩을 메고 노트북을 들었어요.
Today I carried a backpack on my back and a laptop in my hand.
메다 (sling on) vs 들다 (hold in hand) — two carrying verbs
nuance: 가방 is a loanword (originally from Japanese かばん, ultimately tied to Dutch/Chinese roots) and covers all bags — 책가방 (school bag), 백팩/배낭 (backpack), 핸드백 (handbag), 여행 가방 (suitcase/luggage). The interesting depth for English speakers is the TWO carrying verbs Korean forces you to choose between: 메다 (to sling on the shoulder or back, for backpacks and shoulder bags) versus 들다 (to hold/carry in the hand, for handbags and totes) — English 'carry' makes no such distinction, so saying 가방을 들어요 for a backpack you're actually wearing sounds off. For putting things inside, use 가방에 넣다 (넣다 = insert; destination 에); to specify the interior space say 가방 안에. Don't confuse 가방 with 주머니 (pocket) or 봉투/봉지 (paper/plastic bag from a store). Register is neutral and used by everyone.

Saying 가방에 책이 들어요 for 'a book is in the bag.' Use 가방에 책이 있어요 (existence) or 가방 안에; 들다 here would mean 'to hold.'

usage: 으로 marks the computer as the tool/means
examples: 잠깐만요, 컴퓨터 좀 켤게요.
One moment, let me turn on the computer.
-ㄹ게요 = I'll (do it); 좀 softens; 켜다 for powering on
요즘 컴퓨터가 너무 느려서 답답해요.
These days my computer is so slow it's frustrating.
느리다 + -아서; 답답하다 (stifled/frustrated) about a slow PC
보고서를 컴퓨터로 작성했어요.
I wrote the report on the computer.
으로 = by means of; 작성하다 (draft/write up) for documents
nuance: 컴퓨터 is a loanword (English 'computer') and by default means a desktop or computers in general; a laptop is specifically 노트북 (lit. 'notebook,' a Konglish narrowing — note it does NOT mean a paper notebook, which is 공책), and a tablet is 태블릿. The English-speaker pitfall is the instrumental particle: when the computer is the TOOL you act through, use 으로 (컴퓨터로 일해요 = I work using the computer), not 에 — 'on the computer' in English tempts a location particle. But when an action happens AT the machine as a place, 에서 appears (컴퓨터에서 파일을 찾아요 = I look for a file on the computer). For power, the verbs are 켜다 (on) / 끄다 (off), the same pair used for lights and the TV. Don't confuse 컴퓨터 with 모니터 (the monitor screen) or 본체 (the tower/main unit). Register is neutral.

Using 노트북 to mean a paper notebook. 노트북 = laptop; a writing notebook is 공책 or 노트.
Saying 컴퓨터를 열어요 to mean 'turn on the computer.' Powering on is 컴퓨터를 켜요 (켜다). 열다 (open) is for files/programs or doors, not booting up.

usage: to make a call on the phone
으로 marks the phone as the means
to set the phone to silent
examples: 휴대폰 배터리가 다 됐어요.
My phone battery is dead.
배터리가 다 되다 = battery is used up; set phrase
수업 중에는 휴대폰을 무음으로 해 주세요.
During class please set your phone to silent.
-는 중에 = during; 무음으로 하다 = put on silent
휴대폰으로 길을 찾았어요.
I found the way using my phone.
으로 = by means of the phone; 길을 찾다 = find the way
nuance: 휴대폰 is Sino-Korean 携帶 ('carry/portable') + the loanword 폰 ('phone'), literally 'carry-phone,' and it's the standard term; in everyday speech Koreans equally say 핸드폰 (Konglish 'hand-phone') or just 폰, while 스마트폰 specifies a smartphone and 전화 alone usually means a landline or 'a phone call.' The English-speaker pitfall is again the instrumental: when the phone is the tool for an action use 으로 (휴대폰으로 전화해요, 휴대폰으로 찍어요), not 에 — 'on my phone' misleads you toward a location particle. Note 전화하다 already contains 'phone,' so you don't repeat it: say 전화해요, not 휴대폰을 전화해요; if you want to name the device, it's 휴대폰으로 전화해요. To charge is 충전하다, and a dead battery is 배터리가 다 됐어요 (set expression). Register is neutral; 폰 is the most casual.

Using 충전하다 wrongly as 휴대폰에 충전해요. The phone is the object charged: 휴대폰을 충전해요 (object 을).

usage: to open the door with a key
으로 marks the key as the tool
to grab/take the key (don't forget it)
챙기다 collocation for not forgetting to take it
examples: 열쇠로 자물쇠를 열었어요.
I opened the lock with the key.
으로 = by means of the key; 자물쇠 (padlock) is its partner word
집 열쇠를 또 잃어버렸어요.
I lost my house key again.
잃어버리다 → 잃어버렸어요; 또 = again, a common lament
나갈 때 열쇠 꼭 챙기세요.
Be sure to grab your key when you go out.
챙기다 = remember to take; 꼭 = without fail
nuance: 열쇠 is a pure native Korean compound from the verb 열- ('to open') + 쇠 ('metal/iron'), literally an 'open-metal,' i.e. the metal thing that opens — a lovely transparent etymology, and its natural partner is 자물쇠 ('lock-metal,' a padlock/lock). It refers to a physical metal key; modern Korean homes mostly use a 도어록 (door lock keypad) or 번호키 (number/PIN key), so for an apartment you may hear 비밀번호 (passcode) rather than 열쇠. The English-speaker pitfall is the instrumental particle: a key is a TOOL, so 'open the door WITH a key' is 열쇠로 문을 열어요 (으로 = by means of), never 열쇠에. The verb for losing it is 잃어버리다 (lose irretrievably), and the handy verb 챙기다 means 'remember to take it with you.' Figuratively 열쇠 can also mean 'the key/solution' to a problem (문제의 열쇠), just like English. Register is neutral.
